description: Divergent, conservative and convergent boundaries: the magmas, structures and landforms each produces.
content_html:
Three Kinds of Plate Boundary

Tectonic plates interact along their edges, and the type of interaction depends on the direction of relative plate motion. There are three fundamental boundary types: divergent plate boundaries, where plates move apart; conservative plate boundaries, where plates slide past each other; and convergent plate boundaries, where plates move toward each other. Each type produces a distinct set of geological structures, magma types, and landforms.

Key Fact

Divergent: new crust created, basaltic magma (Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East African Rift). Conservative: no crust created or destroyed, volcanic activity absent or minimal (San Andreas Fault). Convergent: crust destroyed by subduction, andesitic or granitic magma (Andes, Himalaya).

Divergent Plate Boundaries

Where two plates pull apart, tensional stress allows the lithosphere to thin and fracture. Magma from the underlying mantle rises to fill the gap, cooling to form new oceanic crust. The result is a mid-ocean ridge — an elevated submarine mountain chain running for thousands of kilometres. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge, for example, extends from the Arctic Ocean to near the tip of South Africa, separating the North American and Eurasian plates in the north and the South American and African plates in the south.

The magma produced at a divergent boundary is basaltic magma. Basaltic magma has a low silica content, low viscosity, and high temperature. It erupts relatively quietly, forming pillow lavas on the ocean floor — rounded blobs of basalt chilled rapidly by cold seawater. On land, where divergence is occurring within a continent, the same process creates a rift valley. The East African Rift, which is slowly splitting the African continent, is a present-day example.

The mid-ocean ridge system is offset along its length by transform faults — horizontal fractures that connect offset ridge segments. Earthquakes are frequent at these fractures but volcanism is absent here; the geological activity is lateral grinding, not eruption.

Conservative Plate Boundaries

At a conservative boundary, two plates slide horizontally past each other along a transform fault. No crust is created or destroyed, which is why these boundaries are called “conservative”. The relative motion generates intense shear stress, and when friction prevents the blocks from sliding smoothly, stress accumulates until it is released suddenly as an earthquake. Volcanism is largely absent.

The San Andreas Fault in California is the most studied example. Here the Pacific Plate slides north-west relative to the North American Plate at roughly 5–6 cm per year. The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake both occurred along this system. The fault is visible at the surface as a long, straight valley where the crushed fault zone erodes more rapidly than surrounding rock.

When an oceanic plate meets a continental plate, the denser oceanic plate sinks beneath the continental plate in a process called subduction. The subducting slab descends at an angle into the mantle, creating a deep trench at the surface — the deepest features on Earth. The Mariana Trench in the Pacific reaches over 11,000 m depth.

As the slab descends, it warms and releases water and other volatiles. These fluids rise into the overlying mantle wedge, lowering its melting point and causing partial melting of the mantle rock. The resulting magma is enriched in silica compared to basalt — it becomes andesitic magma, named after the Andes volcanoes. Andesitic magma is more viscous than basaltic magma and erupts more explosively. The volcanoes that form above the subduction zone are arranged in a curved line called an island arc if the overriding plate is oceanic (e.g. Japan, the Aleutians), or a volcanic mountain range on the continental margin if the overriding plate is continental (e.g. the Andes above the Nazca Plate subducting under the South American Plate).

The zone of deep earthquakes along the descending slab is called the Benioff zone. Earthquakes in this zone can occur at depths down to around 700 km, because the cold, rigid slab remains capable of brittle failure at depth. The depth of earthquake foci in the Benioff zone increases with distance from the trench, allowing geologists to infer the dip angle of the subducting slab using seismic tomography.

Continental Collision Zones

A different type of convergent boundary forms when two continental plates collide. Neither plate is dense enough to subduct, so instead the crust is crumpled and thickened into a mountain belt. This is how the Himalaya formed: the Indian part of the Indo-Australian Plate has been colliding with the Eurasian Plate for roughly 50 million years, producing the highest mountain range on Earth. The collision generates intense compressional stress, folding and thrusting the rocks into the complex structures you studied in the first lessons of this unit.

Magma at continent–continent collision zones tends toward a high silica content — granitic magma — generated by partial melting of the thick continental crust. Granitic magma is highly viscous and does not flow easily, so it typically solidifies underground as large granite batholiths rather than erupting at the surface. The large granite masses exposed in Dartmoor and the Scottish Highlands are examples of ancient magma bodies of this type.

Key Fact

Basaltic magma (low silica, low viscosity, quiet eruptions) forms at divergent boundaries. Andesitic magma (intermediate silica, moderate viscosity, explosive) forms at subduction zones. Granitic magma (high silica, high viscosity, rarely erupts) forms at continent–continent collision zones.

Seismic tomography uses the travel times of seismic waves passing through the Earth to build up 3D images of the mantle. Cold subducting slabs transmit seismic waves faster than the surrounding hot mantle, making them visible as high-velocity anomalies descending into the mantle at subduction zones. This technique has confirmed the geometry of subducting slabs and their fate in the deep mantle.

Ocean drilling recovers rock cores directly from the ocean floor. The magnetic signatures of these basalt cores confirm the spreading rate and polarity history inferred from surface magnetic surveys. Core samples also record changes in ocean chemistry and biological productivity over millions of years, providing an independent check on the plate-tectonic timeline.

Topography of the Ocean Floor

The plate tectonic system creates a characteristic pattern of ocean-floor topography. Mid-ocean ridges rise to about 2,000–3,000 m above the surrounding ocean floor. On either side of the ridge, the ocean floor deepens progressively as the crust ages, cools, and contracts — creating the flat, sediment-covered abyssal plain. At convergent boundaries, the slab descends into the deepest trenches. This systematic depth variation — ridge → abyssal plain → trench — reflects the age and thermal state of the ocean floor, exactly as predicted by sea-floor spreading.
exam_tip_html: Questions on plate boundaries often ask you to link a named location to the correct boundary type and geological products. Practise the triplets: boundary type → named example → geological product. For the 6-mark QER, examiners expect you to name at least three pieces of evidence and explain how each supports the conclusion — not just list them. For magma type questions, the key variable is silica content: low (basaltic, divergent), intermediate (andesitic, subduction), high (granitic, continental collision). Never confuse “conservative” (plates slide past, no volcanism) with “convergent” (plates collide, subduction).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Divergent boundaries produce mid-ocean ridges and rift valleys; tensional stress; basaltic magma with low silica content and low viscosity. Example: Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
  • Conservative boundaries produce large transform faults with intense earthquake activity but no volcanism. Example: San Andreas Fault (Pacific and North American plates).
  • Convergent boundaries produce subduction zones (trenches, Benioff zones, island arcs, andesitic magma) when oceanic meets continental crust (e.g. Andes/Nazca), and mountain belts with granitic intrusions when two continental plates collide (e.g. Himalaya/Indo-Australian and Eurasian plates).

practice_questions.text:
At which plate boundary type is new oceanic crust created?
A) Conservative
B) Convergent (subduction)
C) Continent–continent collision
D) Divergent
Name the zone of deep earthquakes that follows the path of a subducting plate into the mantle.
Describe two differences between the geological activity at a divergent plate boundary and a conservative plate boundary.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks (2 per comparison, 1 for naming, 1 for giving both sides):
• Divergent: volcanic activity occurs (basaltic magma erupts at ridges); conservative: little or no volcanic activity [2]
• Divergent: new oceanic crust is created; conservative: no crust is created or destroyed [2]
Accept: divergent produces rift valleys / ridges; conservative produces large strike-slip faults [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how andesitic magma is produced above a subduction zone.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• The subducting oceanic plate warms and releases water/volatiles as it descends [1]
• These fluids rise into the overlying mantle wedge, lowering its melting point and causing partial melting [1]
• The resulting magma is enriched in silica compared to basalt, producing andesitic magma [1]

practice_questions.text: A mid-ocean ridge is spreading at a half-rate of 3.5 cm per year. Calculate how far apart two points on opposite plates will be after 2 million years. Express your answer in kilometres. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Full spreading rate = 2 × 3.5 = 7 cm/year. Distance = 7 cm/yr × 2,000,000 yr = 14,000,000 cm = 140 km [2 marks: 1 for doubling the half-rate, 1 for correct final answer with units]. Accept: 140 km.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the geological evidence that would allow a geologist to distinguish between an ocean–continent convergent boundary and a continent–continent collision zone. Consider the structures, magmas, and topographic features produced at each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Compares structures (trench + island arc vs mountain belt without trench), magma types (andesitic, explosive at subduction; granitic, intrusive at collision), topography (deep trench vs high plateau/mountain range), seismicity (Benioff zone deep earthquakes at subduction; shallower earthquakes at collision); gives real examples (Andes/Nazca vs Himalaya/Indo-Australian); evaluates which features are most diagnostic; reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure: Correctly identifies at least three distinguishing features across the two boundary types with examples; some evaluation.
Developing: Identifies one or two differences; limited evidence; little evaluation.
Emerging: Partial understanding of one boundary type; no comparison.

At a conservative plate boundary, the two plates move _____ past each other, generating intense earthquakes.

right: Large transform fault, frequent earthquakes, no volcanoes
Deep ocean trench and Benioff zone

flashcard_questions.q: What type of magma erupts at divergent plate boundaries?
flashcard_questions.a: Basaltic magma — low silica, low viscosity.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of magma erupts above a subduction zone?
flashcard_questions.a: Andesitic magma — intermediate silica, more viscous and explosive.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of magma forms at continent–continent collision zones?
flashcard_questions.a: Granitic magma — high silica, highly viscous, rarely erupts at surface.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge an example of?
flashcard_questions.a: A divergent plate boundary between the North American and Eurasian plates.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the San Andreas Fault an example of?
flashcard_questions.a: A conservative plate boundary between the Pacific and North American plates.

flashcard_questions.q: Which two plates are colliding to form the Himalaya?
flashcard_questions.a: The Indo-Australian Plate and the Eurasian Plate.
A zone of deep earthquake foci tracing the path of a subducting plate into the mantle.
A curved chain of volcanic islands formed above a subduction zone.
When only part of a rock body melts, producing magma enriched in silica.
A broad, flat, sediment-covered area of deep ocean floor away from ridges and trenches.

flashcard_questions.q: What is seismic tomography used for?
flashcard_questions.a: To image the Earth's interior using earthquake wave travel times.

flashcard_questions.q: At a conservative boundary, is new crust created or destroyed?
flashcard_questions.a: Neither — no crust is created or destroyed.

glossary_terms.definition: A plate boundary where two plates move apart from each other, allowing magma to rise and create new oceanic crust.
A plate boundary where two plates move past each other horizontally with no crust created or destroyed.
A plate boundary where two plates move toward each other, resulting in subduction, mountain building, or both.
A continuous underwater mountain chain marking a divergent plate boundary where new oceanic crust is created.
Magma or lava with a low silica content (around 45–52%), characterised by low viscosity and high temperature, produced at divergent boundaries and oceanic hot spots.
An elongated lowland valley formed where tensional stress pulls the lithosphere apart and a central block drops down between parallel normal faults.
A large-scale strike-slip fault occurring at a conservative plate boundary, where two plates grind past each other horizontally.
The process by which a denser oceanic plate sinks beneath a less dense continental (or oceanic) plate at a convergent boundary.
A long, narrow, very deep depression in the ocean floor where an oceanic plate is being subducted.
The process by which only some of a rock body melts when exposed to heat or a change in pressure, producing magma that is enriched in silica relative to the source rock.
Magma or lava with an intermediate silica content (around 57–63%), characteristic of volcanic arcs at subduction zones.
A curved chain of volcanic islands formed above a subduction zone where oceanic crust is consumed beneath oceanic crust.
A zone of earthquake foci that dips steeply from an oceanic trench into the mantle, marking the path of a subducting plate.
Magma or lava with a high silica content (around 70% or more), forming granite when intrusive and rhyolite when extrusive; highly viscous and associated with the most explosive eruptions.
A technique using earthquake waves to image the internal structure of the Earth, similar to a medical CT scan.
Scientific drilling of the ocean floor to retrieve cores of basalt and sediment used to study the age and composition of the oceanic crust.
A broad, flat area of the deep ocean floor away from mid-ocean ridges and trenches, formed from old, cool oceanic crust covered by sediment.
